blocks.text: 1. Semi-Supervised Learning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848512-465151137.png

Supervised Learning, covered two topics ago, needs every single training example labeled with its correct answer. Unsupervised Learning, covered in the previous topic, needs no labels at all. Semi-Supervised Learning sits directly between these two extremes.

It combines a small number of labeled examples with a much larger pool of unlabeled ones, a genuinely practical compromise for the common, real-world situation where fully labeling an entire dataset simply is not feasible, but some labeled data is still genuinely available to work with.
2. Why Full Labeling Often Is Not Practical

blocks.alt: Why Full Labeling Often Is Not Practical
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848513-831778508.png

Full labeling often is not practical for genuine, concrete reasons. Labeling can require genuine human expertise, a doctor diagnosing an X-ray for instance, work that is inherently slow and directly limited by how many qualified experts are actually available to do it.

Labeling can also require manually reviewing an enormous volume of data, simply too much data for any team to realistically label every single example by hand within a reasonable amount of time or budget, exactly the labeling cost first raised in the Supervised Learning topic.
3. The Core Idea
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848513-513765827.png

The core idea behind Semi-Supervised Learning is that a small labeled set teaches the model the basic, correct shape of the answer, exactly what a correct prediction should actually look like for this particular problem.

The much larger unlabeled set then reveals the data's broader, underlying structure, information a small labeled set alone simply cannot capture on its own. Combining both lets the model learn considerably more than the labeled set alone could ever teach it in isolation, genuinely the entire point of this approach.
4. Self-Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848513-757079314.png

A common technique called self-training starts by training an initial model on just the small labeled set available, exactly as a standard Supervised Learning model would be trained. That initial model then predicts labels for the unlabeled data, generating a guess for every example that does not already have a known, correct answer.

The most confident of these predictions get added to the labeled set as if they were genuinely, actually true, and the model gets retrained on this larger, now-expanded labeled set. This entire process then repeats, gradually growing the effectively labeled portion of the dataset with each round.

blocks.text: 5. Label Spreading
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848745-373484983.png

Another common technique, label spreading, connects directly back to the closeness concept already touched on in the Unsupervised Learning topic's clustering discussion. Labels propagate outward from the small set of already-labeled points to nearby, genuinely similar unlabeled points.

Points that sit far away from any labeled example remain considerably more uncertain under this approach, since there is no nearby labeled point to propagate a confident label from. This technique leans directly on the data's own natural structure, letting genuinely similar points share label information with each other.
6. A Genuine Risk: Reinforcing Mistakes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848747-450985304.png

A genuine risk unique to this approach is that a confidently wrong prediction can get added to the labeled set as if it were actually true, and that single mistake can then reinforce itself across further training rounds, since the model keeps learning from its own earlier, incorrect guess.

Careful confidence thresholds, only accepting predictions the model is genuinely very sure about, help limit how many mistakes get accepted this way. This is not a perfect safeguard against every possible error, but it is a meaningful, genuinely practical mitigation worth applying whenever self-training or a similar technique gets used.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This self-reinforcing mistake risk is precisely why confidence thresholds matter so much in self-training. Accepting only a model's most confident predictions as new labels considerably reduces, though never fully eliminates, this genuine risk.

blocks.text: 7. Familiar, Real-World Examples

Semi-Supervised Learning already shows up in familiar systems. Medical image diagnosis, with only a handful of expert-labeled scans genuinely available, is a classic example, since vastly more unlabeled scans exist than any medical team could realistically label by hand within a reasonable timeframe.

Web page classification, with only a small, manually categorized sample of pages, is another classic example, since billions of web pages exist in total, and only a tiny fraction of them ever actually get manually labeled by a human reviewer.

blocks.text: 8. When Semi-Supervised Learning Genuinely Shines
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442848748-236392744.png

Semi-Supervised Learning genuinely shines when a small labeled set alone underperforms, when there is simply too little labeled data for a standard Supervised Learning approach to generalize well on its own. Adding unlabeled data in this situation provides genuinely useful additional signal the labeled set alone could not offer.

It also shines when a large amount of unlabeled data is already readily available anyway, data that is cheap to include in training but that would have been expensive, or simply impractical, to fully label from scratch, letting that already-available data get put to genuine, productive use.
9. Recognizing When to Reach for This Approach

Semi-Supervised Learning is worth reaching for whenever labeling is genuinely expensive, slow, or requires scarce specialized expertise, exactly the constraint already covered throughout this topic, since it directly addresses that specific practical limitation.

It is also worth reaching for whenever a large pool of unlabeled data already sits unused somewhere, Semi-Supervised Learning puts that otherwise-idle data to genuine, productive work, rather than leaving it on the table simply because it was never manually labeled.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements a simple self-training loop, starting from a small labeled set and gradually expanding it using the model's own confident predictions.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.semi_supervised import SelfTrainingClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 2))
y_true = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)

y = y_true.copy()
unlabeled_mask = rng.rand(300) > 0.1  # only 10% of examples start out labeled
y[unlabeled_mask] = -1  # -1 marks an example as unlabeled

labeled_count = np.sum(y != -1)
print(f"Starting with only {labeled_count} labeled examples out of {len(y)} total")

base_model = SVC(probability=True, kernel="linear")
self_training_model = SelfTrainingClassifier(base_model, threshold=0.9)
self_training_model.fit(X, y)

final_accuracy = (self_training_model.predict(X) == y_true).mean()
print(f"Final accuracy after self-training: {final_accuracy:.2%}")
print("The model expanded its effective labeled set using its own confident predictions")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The threshold=0.9 parameter in this example only accepts predictions the model is at least 90 percent confident about as new labels, exactly the confidence-threshold mitigation covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Semi-Supervised Learning sits between Supervised and Unsupervised Learning, combining a small labeled set with a larger unlabeled pool.
Full labeling often is not practical due to scarce expert time or an overwhelming volume of data.
A small labeled set teaches the correct answer shape; a larger unlabeled set reveals broader structure.
Self-training trains on labeled data, predicts on unlabeled data, and adds confident predictions as new labels.
Label spreading propagates labels outward to nearby similar points through the data's own structure.
A confidently wrong prediction can reinforce itself; confidence thresholds help limit this genuine risk.
Medical image diagnosis and web page classification are classic, familiar Semi-Supervised examples.
This approach shines when a small labeled set alone underperforms and abundant unlabeled data is already available.
